title: Methodus generalior numeros quosvis satis grandes perscrutandi utrum sint primi necne?

deep.reconstruction:
This page carries out the factoring test announced in §§1–2 on the worked example N = 10003. The test rests on one fact: if a suitable (idoneal) form represents N in two different ways, N is composite, and the factors can be read off from the two representations.

§2 (end): with N = aa + λbb already known, one writes N = xx + λyy. One then fixes the parities of x and y and imposes the condition that N − xx is divisible by λ (or that N − λyy is a square). This produces new quadratic expressions in an unknown that must be squares, split into cases by parity.

§3: N = 10003 = 100² + 3·1², so λ = 3. Since N ≡ 3 (mod 8), y cannot be even, because then xx would be ≡ 5 or 1 (mod 8) as required by N, which fails here. So y is odd, 3yy ≡ 3 (mod 8), and xx ≡ 0 (mod 8). Hence 4 | x.

§4: with y = 1 + 2a, N − 3yy = 10000 − 12a − 12a² must be divisible by 16. This forces a(a+1) ≡ 0 (mod 4). Euler then puts y = 1 + 8a, where a is allowed to be negative so that y ≡ ±1 (mod 8) is covered. This gives 625 − 3a − 12a² = (x/4)².

§5: a even. The left side is odd, so it must be ≡ 1 (mod 8), which forces a = 8b. Then 625 − 24b − 768b² is a square only for b = 0, the known representation.

§6: a = 4c + 1 gives 610 − 108c − 192c² ≡ 2 (mod 4), which is never a square.

§7: a = 4d − 1 gives 616 + 84d − 192d², i.e. 154 + 21d − 48d² = (x/8)². The values of 48d² ± 21d below 154 are 27, 69 and 150. Only 154 − 150 = 4 is a square, at d = 2. So a = 7, y = 57, x = 16.

§8: the second representation is 10003 = 16² + 3·57². Then (a+x)/(y+b) = 116/58 = 2 and (y−b)/(a−x) = 56/84 = 2/3, so p = 2, q = 3. Hence 3p² + q² = 21; removing the factor 3 leaves 7. Indeed 10003 = 7·1429, and 1429 is prime.

§9 begins the justification: one needs a form such as 3xx + yy for which a single representation guarantees primality, i.e. Euler's idoneal (convenient) numbers.

All arithmetic checks out.
errors: §4: 'numerum a denuo per 4 divisibilem esse debere' is imprecise. The condition is a(a+1) ≡ 0 (mod 4), i.e. a ≡ 0 or 3 (mod 4). The substitution y = 1+8a still covers every case only because a may be negative, which gives y ≡ −1 ≡ 7 (mod 8) up to sign. Euler does use negative values tacitly (d = ±, 48dd ± 21d), so nothing is lost.

Inconsistency with §1 (previous page): there Euler says λpp + qq is the factor 'vel ipsam, vel ejus semissem, vel quadrantem'. In the example, 21 must instead be divided by λ = 3. Also, the §1 parametrization (a+x = λmp, y+b = mq) gives a non-integral m here (m = 58/3). §10 (next page) corrects this by allowing division by α, β and 2.

§9: the claim that numbers represented only once by 3xx+yy are prime needs the usual provisos (primitive representations, gcd(x,3y) = 1, and the exceptions for squares, powers of 2, etc.). Euler adds these only in §12.

ideas.what: Factoring N from two distinct representations N = a²+λb² = x²+λy² via gcd-type fractions (a±x)/(b±y)
ideas.modern_name: Euler's factorization method (two representations by a quadratic form)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (sum-of-two-squares version, E228 era; general forms in idoneal-number papers)
ideas.where_published: E228 and the idoneal-number papers of the 1770s–80s (E708, E715, E718, E719, E725)

ideas.what: Sieving candidate y by congruences mod 8/16 and parity case splits to reduce the search for a second representation
ideas.modern_name: Exclusion/sieve method for representations by binary quadratic forms
ideas.where_published: Euler's idoneal-number papers; Gauss DA Sect. VI

ideas.what: Primality certification by uniqueness of representation by an idoneal form (3xx+yy)
ideas.modern_name: Idoneal numbers / one class per genus
ideas.where_published: E708, E715, E719, E725; see Weil, Number Theory: An approach through history

deep.surprise_reason: This is a correct, routine worked example (10003 = 7·1429) of Euler's well-known idoneal-number factoring method. The only point of note is a small slip in §1 about which divisor (2, 4 or λ) to remove, which Euler himself repairs in §10.
transcription_corrections: §8: the '[?]' marks can be removed. The image reads '3p/q = 116/58 = 2, 56/84 = 2/3' (i.e. (a+x)/(y+b) = 2 and (y−b)/(a−x) = 2/3), which is arithmetically correct.
